% numbers.tex (generated by experiments/icpc/make_numbers.py). Do not type numbers by hand.
\begin{abstract}
Program slicing helps developers understand and debug code, and it has been proposed for quantum
programs by reusing the classical slicing criterion and graph reachability over a quantum program
dependence graph. No definition of quantum dependence has been checked against the semantics of
quantum programs. We define it semantically, as the set of operations where a change can alter a
qubit's state for some input, and use this ground truth to evaluate dependence definitions on
\numNPairs{} circuit--qubit pairs from three benchmark suites, \numFamCircuits{} circuits with known
structure, and \numRqThreeUnits{} seeded faults. Even the full classical program dependence graph, with data and
control dependence, gives wrong slices for \numCpdgUnsoundPct{} of the pairs, because it misses the
quantum dependence of a gate on its control qubit (phase kickback). Following entanglement, as the proposed quantum program dependence graph does, is
sound but keeps \numRqOneYzSize{} of the circuit. Adding quantum dependence, so that every multi-qubit gate reads and writes all its qubits, keeps
\numRqOneLcSize{}, is complete against the ground truth, and stays correct on every tested input, and
its soundness is machine-checked. Commutation pruning shrinks these slices further and stays correct
on all random inputs. State-based pruning shrinks them by \numHTwoRelative{}, but only for the input
it was computed on. It removes the faulty operation in \numCQFour{} of the seeded faults and lowers
the fault-localization accuracy of three language models by up to
\numTTwoMaxDrop{}~percentage points. A criterion over all affected qubits recovers \numCQFourRecovered{}
of these faults. Quantum dependence is not entanglement, and the results give tool builders a sound,
input-independent dependence rule and a slicing criterion that fits quantum state.
\end{abstract}
